hints.quote: Know the types of implants (endosseous, transosteal...), and be able to recognize them by x-ray/photos.
hints.take: Endosteal (root form, blade, ramus frame), eposteal/subperiosteal, transosteal (TMI); plus Dr. Mueninghoff's seven types. The picture questions practice recognizing them.

hints.quote: There are seven. And those are the things that you've got to remember what they are. And out of this entire lecture, that's something that you really need to know.
hints.take: Subperiosteal, endodontic stabilizer, transosseous, intramucosal insert, blade/plate form, ramus frame, root form.

hints.quote: As far as any kind of exam is concerned, you have to recognize the types of implants. We don't worry about the other things.
hints.take: Recognize each type; the stories are context.

hints.quote: The advantages and disadvantages of the root form, don't worry about that.
hints.take: Skip the root form's pros and cons from his slide.

hints.quote: You can read it later on. You don't need to memorize all that. You just need to recognize what a ramus frame is.
hints.take: Recognition, not the details on the slide.

hints.quote: Surface treatment of implant; machined surface vs smooth surface; Ti alloy vs cp Ti.
hints.take: Additive (TPS, HA, microspheres) vs subtractive (acid etch, blasting); TiUnite, SLA, RBT. Machined screw beats smooth cylinder. Ti-6Al-4V is stronger than CP Ti (grade 4).

hints.quote: Periodontal attachment vs peri-implant attachment.
hints.take: JE on titanium with hemidesmosomes only apically, from oral epithelium; circular and parallel fibers, none inserting; more collagen, fewer fibroblasts; biologic width 3.08 mm vs 2.04-2.91 mm.

hints.quote: One stage vs two stage approach, and the corresponding components (healing abutment/ cover screw).
hints.take: Two-stage (Brånemark): cover screw, submerged 3-6 months, second surgery for the healing abutment. One-stage (Schroeder): healing abutment from the start.

hints.quote: Definition of successful osseointegration.
hints.take: Direct attachment of bone to an alloplastic material without intervening connective tissue (Chavali); Brånemark 1969 and Albrektsson 1991 (Geisinger).

hints.quote: How do you diagnose a failing implant? And this will be definitely on your quiz or exam.
hints.take: Mobility, percussion pain, infection, radiolucency, bone loss; bone loss beyond half the implant = failure.

hints.quote: I'm not going to ask you a question about which are those, but I'll ask you a question about single-stage surgery and two-stage surgery.
hints.take: Know the two approaches and their parts; not the immediate-loading cases.

hints.quote: I'm going to ask you this question, if it's the grading of different titanium.
hints.take: CP grades rise in strength; the alloy is strongest; which system uses which.

hints.quote: Every implant system has their own surface treatment. And I want you to remember this... So this will also be on my exam.
hints.take: TiUnite (Nobel), SLA (Straumann), RBT (BioHorizons).

hints.quote: The most important thing, I'm not going to ask you to do your examination with some of this, [which cell] is what and what not.
hints.take: The cells of the healing video aren't tested; the stability drop is.

hints.quote: The way to distribute adverse forces on implants; vertical and horizontal cantilevers.
hints.take: Avoid both; more implants, smaller table, splinting; augment or add implants for a vertical cantilever; moment = force x distance.

hints.quote: The biting force between different types of dentitions (natural dentition vs implant removable...).
hints.take: Implant-supported FPD > natural dentition > implant-retained denture > complete denture.

hints.quote: Bone quality (Misch classification); Wolff's law.
hints.take: D1 anterior mandible, D2 posterior mandible, D3 anterior maxilla, D4 posterior maxilla. Bone remodels to the loads on it.

hints.quote: Problem of splinting natural tooth with implant.
hints.take: Tooth moves 25-100 µm, implant 3-5 µm: the implant takes the force.

hints.quote: Goal for implant occlusion.
hints.take: Lighter than the teeth; long axis, low cusps, small table, no excursive contacts; shimstock out of contact in MI (vs a tooth), drags not tears (two implants).

hints.quote: Among the following forces which are the most favorable or conducive to the bone... the most favorable would be compressive forces, the least favorable would be shearing forces. Okay, let's say giveaway for the quiz.
hints.take: Compression > tension > shear.

hints.quote: Remember never connect an implant and natural teeth. This will be your exam question.
hints.take: The PDL mismatch.

hints.quote: I do not have this listed but I want you to remember if you can write it down. D1 bone anterior mandible...
hints.take: Misch D1-D4 locations.

hints.quote: I want you to remember the stress is force per unit area.
hints.take: Stress = force/area; splinting spreads it.

hints.quote: Crown:implant ratio.
hints.take: More forgiving than 1:1, but ~2:1 (15 mm crown) means more screw loosening, fracture, bone loss: splint.

hints.quote: Prefabricated (stock) vs custom abutments.
hints.take: Stock: straight, uniform margin, subtractive adjustment only (TiBase, solid, anatomic). Custom: patient contour, retention, traces the tissue; always engaging.

hints.quote: Torque requirement for different implants and components.
hints.take: Nobel 35 Ncm (3.0 mm: 15), Straumann 35, BioHorizons 30; fingers ~5. Immediate loading: insertion 25-40 Ncm or ISQ >70.

hints.quote: Internal connection vs external/ conical connection vs non-conical connection.
hints.take: External: screw loosening, tolerates divergence. Internal: less microgap. Conical: less bone loss, fewer prosthetic complications, same survival. Morse taper = cold welding.

hints.quote: Primary stability/ secondary stability/ stability dip.
hints.take: Primary falls as secondary rises; the dip comes weeks after placement.

hints.quote: Distance (mm) around the implant: to the bone/ to the tooth/ to the other implant.
hints.take: Depth 3-4 mm below the gingival margin; 1.5 mm to a tooth; 3 mm to an implant; 2 mm facial (anterior/immediate); 1 mm lingual.

hints.quote: Engaging vs non-engaging abutment.
hints.take: Engaging locks on the hex/grooves; non-engaging spins. Single crown: engaging. Cement FPD: engaging. Screw FPD: non-engaging.

hints.quote: Screw-retained vs cement-retained.
hints.take: Screw: one piece, retrievable, no cement. Cement: separate, passive, esthetic. Facial implant: cement (or angled channel).

hints.quote: EBC zones.
hints.take: C (1-1.5 mm, straight, abutment), B (concave), E (1 mm under margin, esthetics). Concave lets the margin creep coronally; convex pushes it apically.

hints.quote: Implant placement/ loading timeline (immediate placement, immediate loading...).
hints.take: ITI 2018: placement immediate / early (4-8, 12-16 wk) / late (>6 mo); loading immediate (<1 wk) / early (1 wk-2 mo) / conventional (>2 mo).

hints.quote: For my exam, if you can totally understand what I have on the slide, you should have no problem. I don't ask you to study on the textbook.
hints.take: The slides are the source.

hints.quote: Look at the stickers, very important. Stickers, stickers.
hints.take: The BioHorizons platform trap.

hints.quote: So these numbers I want to remember, okay? There's not too many signs inside, just remember, that's a rule of thumb.
hints.take: 1.5 mm, 3 mm, 2 mm, 1 mm, 3-4 mm.

hints.quote: So those are the common number you will need to memorize... 35, 30, when do we use 35, when we use 30.
hints.take: Straumann/Nobel 35, BioHorizons 30.

hints.quote: If you want to do the single crown for the implant, always use engaging.
hints.take: There's no non-engaging option for a single crown.

hints.quote: Seven millimeters from the implant platform, the bone to the top of [the crown] is what you need for the cement retained as a very, very minimal requirement.
I don't think I gotta test you here, but based on the consensus, they have some kind of different measurement about different approach.
hints.take: The ITI evidence grid itself is less likely; the definitions are on the hint list.

hints.quote: This is an exam question. There are a lot of slides in this PowerPoint that is an exam question. The screw retain, this 5 mm rule, interocclusal space is an exam question.
hints.take: 5 mm or less: screw-retained.

hints.quote: The risk of peri-implantitis is an exam question.
hints.take: Much higher with cement-retained crowns.

hints.quote: Difference between a custom abutment and a prefabricated abutment is a custom UCLA abutment... So a lot of exam questions here.
hints.take: Stock vs custom; UCLA (cast) vs CAD/CAM.

hints.quote: This next exam question: what is information you have to give the lab when you send your case out.
hints.take: Mounted casts + soft tissue model, system, diameter, soft tissue height, order form.

hints.quote: This is an example question again. Now this particular slide we want you to know that there are three different implant systems.
hints.take: Nobel conical connection, Straumann bone level, BioHorizons internal.

hints.quote: This is just my classification, please don't take it as something from the literature.
hints.take: His abutments-by-stage list is a teaching aid.

hints.quote: At the second floor and at the undergraduate level you don't need it.
hints.take: The multi-unit abutment (All-on-4).

hints.quote: Dr. Givan: be able to answer the details on his study guide.
hints.take: His "what do I want you to know" sheets: the three phases, modalities, ALARA, PA and pan pros and cons, CT vs CBCT, HU, artifacts, scan templates (this lecture), and the physics (next lecture).

hints.quote: That's why we speak of implant planning overall as being a prosthetically driven but biologically balanced process.
hints.take: The theme of his lecture and study guide.

hints.quote: Alara is the lowest achievable dose that you need to know.
hints.take: As low as reasonably achievable.

hints.quote: PAs are by far the number one go-to that we would want to have.
hints.take: Baseline and routine follow-up of the crest.

hints.quote: Slightly different, but still correct definition than previous lecture, know both!!!
hints.take: Hounsfield units: a scale of radiodensity; relative attenuation vs air and water. (His study guide.)

hints.quote: I want to kind of make sure we pull out two important topics and good takeaways from this of saying why do I have trouble imaging, particularly around a lot of metal.
hints.take: Compton scatter and beam hardening around metal.

hints.quote: It's important to remember that bit depth is one of the things that... the higher the bit depth...
hints.take: Dynamic range / gray scale resolution, and why it drives cost.

hints.quote: In CBCT the HU scale is unreliable (but still helpful) for treatment decisions, such as for immediate loading.
hints.take: From his study guide.

hints.quote: Early failure of implants.
hints.take: Surgical failures (heat >47°C, force, contamination), early occlusal overload, impaired wound healing, poor bone metabolism.

hints.quote: Esthetic risk factor.
hints.take: High: heavy smoker, reduced immunity, high expectations, high lip line, thin scalloped tissue, triangular crowns, acute infection, ≥7 mm bone to contact, restored neighbors, 2+ teeth, soft tissue defect, vertical deficiency.

hints.quote: Definition of successful osseointegration.
hints.take: Brånemark 1969 (light microscopic contact) and Albrektsson & Sennerby 1991 (living bone, load-carrying); about 60% contact, 0.3 mm from the interface, 6 weeks-3 months.

hints.quote: Peri-implant disease: factors and treatment outcomes.
hints.take: Patient, implant, site, prosthetic and surgical factors; 75% unresolved or recurring in 5 years, so prevention.

hints.quote: If bone temperature gets above 47 degrees Celsius... we get thermal necrosis that can be catastrophic.
hints.take: Sequential drills and irrigation.

hints.quote: About 75% of peri-implantitis cases that we attempt to treat are either not treated or recur within a five-year period. So we're terrible at it.
hints.take: Prevention is the treatment.

hints.quote: Implants over 13 and a half millimeters actually have a higher failure rate than implants between eight and 13 millimeters. Longer and wider is not always better.
35 is a threshold to put something transgingival on. An implant that has a stability of less than 15 is considered unstable.
Freehand/ semi-guided/ fully guided/ dynamic guided surgery.
hints.take: No guide; pilot-drill guide (UAB's usual); a guide for every drill (CBCT + digital wax-up); real-time navigation.

hints.quote: Surgically vs prosthetically driven surgery.
hints.take: Placed where the bone is vs where the restoration needs it; it must be restorable.

hints.quote: Implant can be placed almost everywhere (except on root, nerve, air). But you need to be able to restore it.
hints.take: Prosthetically driven (and surgically acceptable).

hints.quote: This is what we do most of the time in UAB student clinic.
hints.take: Semi-guided (pilot) surgery.

hints.quote: CBCT is the current standard of care for most implant cases.
hints.take: The lecture's summary.

evolution: Seven types: subperiosteal, endodontic stabilizer, transosseous, intramucosal insert, blade/plate form, ramus frame, root form
Know them well enough to recognize: "that's something you really need to know"
Bone integrates with titanium OXIDE (a ceramic); gold has almost none
Brånemark: orthopedic surgeon; Carl Misch popularized implants in the U.S.
Subperiosteal: on bone under periosteum, two surgeries, gross bone destruction when it fails
Endo stabilizer: through the root canal; stainless steel + poor seal
Intramucosal: denture buttons in mucosal holes; out only a few hours
Ramus frame (Roberts brothers): one piece, symphysis to both rami, lower denture; Ford Turner's lasted 10-25 yrs
Blade (Roberts; Linkow holes; Cranin anchor): fibrous layer, tied to a tooth
Transosteal: Germany 1930s; Bosker TMI through anterior mandible; bone grew behind it
Hollow baskets: bone grows only ~0.5 mm in; IMZ insert too mobile; sapphire broke
About 173 implant companies; identify one at whatimplantisthat.com
intro: Implant: alloplastic, under mucosa/periosteum, on or in bone, retains and supports a prosthesis
Osseointegration: direct bone attachment, no intervening connective tissue (Brånemark, rabbits, 1952)
Primary = initial mechanical lock; secondary = remodeling (from ~4-6 wk, continues after loading)
Clinic wait: 4 months mandible, 6 months maxilla
Two-stage (Brånemark 1985): cover screw, 3-6 mo; one-stage (Schroeder 1996): healing abutment, 3-4 mo
3 weeks for tissue around the healing abutment
Endosteal (one cortical plate: root form, blade, ramus frame), eposteal = subperiosteal, transosteal (both plates, anterior mandible)
Failure signs: mobility, percussion pain, infection, radiolucency, bone loss; bone loss > half the implant = failure
Ti oxide layer; CP Ti grades 1-4 (Grade 4 used); Ti-6Al-4V strongest
BioHorizons = Ti-6Al-4V; Straumann and Nobel = Grade 4 CP
Additive: TPS, HA, microspheres; subtractive: acid etch, blasting
Implant: JE on Ti, hemidesmosomes apical 1/3, from oral epithelium; circular + parallel fibers; BW 3.08 mm (tooth 2.04-2.91)
More collagen, fewer fibroblasts; rigid; no proprioception: light contacts
Two-implant overdenture = standard of care for the edentulous mandible
biomech: Wolff: bone architecture follows external load; adaptive window
Stress = force / area; moment = force x distance
Maxilla: thin cortex, fine trabeculae, force distributing; mandible: thick, coarse, force absorbing
D1 ant mandible, D2 post mandible, D3 ant maxilla, D4 post maxilla
Compression > tension > shear: avoid shear and tension
Failures: attachments 30%, resin veneer 22%, short 17%, soft bone 16%, removable 12%, screw 7-10%, porcelain 7%, metal 3%, implant 1-2%
<10 mm implants fail a bit more; not contraindicated
Sizes: lateral 3, central 3.5, premolar 3.5-4, molar 4.5-6 mm; 1 mm bone each side
More force: young, male, large, parafunction (wear, fractures, exostoses); night guard
High risk: more implants, smaller occlusal table, splint
Don't splint across the arch behind the mental foramina (flexure)
No cantilevers (horizontal or vertical); 25 lb → 75 lb + 50 lb
Vertical cantilever: augment or add implants; FP-1/2/3
Span flexibility rises by the cube
Implant FPD > natural > implant-retained denture > complete denture
Never join implant and tooth: 25-100 µm vs 3-5 µm
Single implant vs tooth: out of contact in MI; two implants: shimstock drags, not tears
Long axis, low cusps, small table, no excursive contacts
terms: Brand ≠ product line; know your systems' platforms
BioHorizons 4.6 mm Internal Plus = 3.5 mm (yellow) platform: check the sticker
Platform switching: narrower abutment, microgap away from bone
External: screw loosening, tolerates divergence; internal: force on implant, less microgap (school = internal)
Tissue level: less bone loss; bone level: room to contour
Tapered: primary stability, avoids anatomy; parallel: surface area
Total = primary + secondary; stability dip weeks out
Fingers ~5 Ncm; Nobel 35 (3.0 mm: 15), Straumann 35, BioHorizons 30
Conical = internal tapered; less microgap, bone loss, prosthetic complications; same survival
Morse taper = cold-weld conical (Ankylos 5.7°)
Cover screw (stage 1, hidden) vs healing abutment (taller, exposed)
Depth 3-4 mm below gingival margin; 1.5 mm to tooth; 3 mm between implants; 2 mm facial; 1 mm lingual
Anterior: lingual (screw-retained possible); posterior: mid-ridge
Engaging (hex, grooves; Straumann RC 4 grooves) vs non-engaging (spins)
Closed tray 99%; open tray more accurate for multiple units
Screw: retrievable, no cement; cement: passive, esthetic, strong
Too facial → cement or angled channel (stripping >15°)
Screwmentable: crown bonded to TiBase outside the mouth
Single crown: engaging. Cement FPD: custom, engaging. Screw FPD: TiBase, non-engaging
Cement molar: 3 - 1 + 4 + 1 = 7 mm; screwmentable 6-7 mm from platform
Crown:implant up to ~2:1 with more complications: splint
C zone 1-1.5 mm straight (abutment); B concave; E 1 mm under margin (esthetics)
Concave E → margin creeps coronally (or buccal implant); convex → apically (or lingual)
Teflon tape, 2 mm, then composite
Verification jig on non-engaging parts; Sheffield one-screw test
ITI: placement immediate / early 4-8 or 12-16 wk / late >6 mo; loading immediate <1 wk / early 1 wk-2 mo / conventional >2 mo
Immediate criteria: intact walls, facial ≥1 mm, thick tissue, no infection, 25-40 Ncm or ISQ >70
Codes: D0367 CBCT, D6190 index, D6010 implant, D6057 custom abutment, D6058 cement crown, D6065 screw crown
prefab: Prefabricated = stock; 99.9% of clinic cases use custom
Stages: cover screw / healing abutment → temporary abutment → final (stock or custom)
Two-stage for smokers and diabetics; one-stage for young, healthy
~3 weeks for tissue around the healing abutment
Healing abutments: heights; narrow for incisors, wide for molars
Temporary: screw (Ti cylinder) or cement (plastic sleeve); non-engaging for bridges
Stock pros: fit, cheap (~$50, sometimes free), strong; cons: must prep, deep margins trap cement, poor emergence
Cuff heights 1-5 mm: measure from the collar; angled stock or custom for a tilted implant
UCLA: plastic sleeve on Ti base, waxed and cast; CAD/CAM: milled
EXAM: ≤5 mm interocclusal space → screw-retained; >5 mm either, unless the hole would show facially → cement
Cement-retained: much higher peri-implantitis risk; often more esthetic
Lab: mounted casts + soft tissue model, system, diameter, soft tissue height, order form
School: Nobel conical, Straumann bone level, BioHorizons internal
imaging: Phase 1: bone quality/quantity/angle, structures, disease; Phase 2: position, healing, abutment; Phase 3: crestal bone for life
Three common: PA, pan, CBCT; ALARA
PA: high resolution; no width, no quantitative quality, distortion
Pan: screening; superimposition, distortion, magnification; up to 30% height error, no width (Reddy 1994)
4-5 mm bearings: vertical ratio, only in the focal area
Tomogram = picture, tomograph = machine, tomography = process
Medical CT: fan beam, fast, helix, supine (claustrophobia, soft tissue collapse, TMJ off)
CBCT: cone beam, slow, 2-D → 3-D, sitting, 5-10x less dose, more Compton scatter
Hounsfield units = radiodensity; not proven to predict stability
CT pros: accurate measures, no distortion, bone profiles, guides, flapless
Remove metal dentures; Ti little artifact, gold a lot
Starburst: sharp density change, sampling (not scatter); beam hardening: black areas
Scan template: shows the proposed teeth; stability; opens VDO slightly
Guide → scan → plan; optional guide → guided surgery
cbct: CBCT = cone beam computed tomography; gantry rotates source + detector
Thermionic emission from the heated cathode; tungsten focal spot ~0.5 mm; 99% heat
Higher kVp → higher energy, more penetration
Characteristic (K-shell) vs Bremsstrahlung (braking near nucleus): polyenergetic beam
Primary filter Al/Cu removes low energy; lead collimator shapes
Attenuation: intensity loss through matter; more with thickness, density, atomic number
Interactions: none, photoelectric, Rayleigh (minor), Compton; PE + Compton matter most
CR: phosphor plate + laser (PAs, not CBCT); indirect DR: x-ray → light → photodiode → signal
Flat panel TFT most common; scintillator, photodiodes (pixels), electronics
Smaller pixels: more resolution, worse SNR; dynamic range = gray scale (bit depth)
ROI = what you need; FoV = cylinder scanned (sets dose); ALARA
Axial, sagittal, coronal; panoramic + cross-sectional; 3-D surface not for measuring
Scatter streaks; beam hardening (cupping, dark bands); motion double contours (head rest, short scan)
HU: air -1000, water 0; unreliable in CBCT
surgery: 178 M missing a tooth; 40 M edentulous; 30% of 65-74; ~5 M implants/yr
Osseointegration: Brånemark 1969 (light microscopic contact); Albrektsson 1991 (living bone, load-carrying)
~60% BIC; stops 0.3 mm from the implant-abutment interface; 6 wk-3 mo
Early failure: surgical (heat, force, contamination), early overload, poor healing, poor bone turnover
Late failure: biologic (mucositis, peri-implantitis), overload, prosthetic
75% of peri-implantitis unresolved or recurs in 5 years: prevention
Mucositis: bleeding/suppuration, deeper pockets, no bone loss beyond remodeling
Peri-implantitis: + progressive bone loss vs the 1-year film; no baseline: ≥3 mm bone and/or PD ≥6 mm + bleeding
Risks: patient, implant, site, prosthetic (cement, overload, contours), surgical
Contraindications: recent MI/stroke, ≥10 cigarettes/day, still growing
>13.5 mm implants fail more than 8-13 mm
Space: C&B 7-8 mm (cement) / 7.5 (screw); OD 10-12; bar 11-14; zirconia 10-12; hybrid ≥15
Esthetic high risk: heavy smoker, high lip line, thin scalloped, triangular, acute infection, ≥7 mm to contact, 2+ teeth, vertical defect
Bone dies above 47°C: sequential drills, irrigation
Last drill narrower than the implant (3.5 mm implant: 2.8 mm drill)
guided: Where: surgically vs prosthetically driven; how: freehand, static guided, dynamic guided
Surgeon finds (or makes) bone; restorative dentist restores
Posterior: middle of the wax-up, long axis; anterior: zenith, lingual above the cingulum
Can't reach ideal: compromise (cement-retained), graft, enameloplasty (plan first)
Freehand: no guide, CBCT still needed, cheap, more error, no restorative input
Semi-guided (pilot): bone unknown, pilot drill only; UAB student clinic's usual
Fully guided: CBCT + digital wax-up, every drill, sleeves + stop keys; accurate, faster surgery; costly, slow prep, "blind surgery"
Tooth-supported most accurate; tissue moves; bone may be distorted
Steps: STL, DICOM, mount/wax up, align, plan, design, print
D6190 $50; D6190GS $225; up to 2 extra crown credits
CBCT = standard of care for most implant cases
